# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to solution to sending, but the look-back window (screen 4) sits between two context screens that carry the same heading and question, so the context step reads as if it restarts.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 ask the same question: 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks about the commercial side. There is no screen for the price (about $1k per site per month, with multi-site and multi-month discounts), none for who pays and decides (the general contractor's operations lead or CFO, not the superintendent), and none for the purchase steps, such as the Procore check and the security review of site videos. The pilot offer on screen 19 therefore comes without any price or buyer having been set.

PRIMARY.order_why: It goes from whether my jobs are on Procore, to what I actually did last week, then the idea, then what I'd do with it, which is how I'd think it through.
PRIMARY.missing: How long the daily log itself takes me after the walks, and whether I've had to pull old logs and photos to back up a delay claim or dispute with the owner. That's why the record has to be accurate. Also whether the notes would go straight into the Procore daily log, or whether I'd still be re-typing them in the trailer.

screens.why5: My two benefits, hours back at the end of the day and action items to the crew the same day, go in as typed and nothing is reworded on this screen.
screens.why7: The screen matches the card's founder list: 1 to 4 benefits, each up to 9 words, one per line, described as what changes compared with today's way, with 'I'm not sure' as the escape that leaves the dimension out.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Fresco does better, it makes sense to check the benefits Keel drafted before it builds the belief it will test.
screens.why2: "Hours back at the end of the day" and "action items to the crew the same day" are exactly how a super talks about the trailer hours and getting punch items out.
screens.why3: Both benefits come straight from what my supers live: hours in the trailer after the walks, and crew items that sit until the next morning.
screens.why4: Two distinct rows, one gain each, no overlap, nothing invented, and my lead benefit (time back, 90% faster) is the first row.
screens.why5: It still means what I pitch: notes done during the walk instead of after, and items texted to the crew right away, with no number I didn't give.
screens.why7: The rows meet the card and the belief joins both with 'and', but its hard case is the bare 'their last daily log' (an occasion, and one Revision 25 renamed to 'site walk') rather than the study's problem clause naming the day it hurt, which the card says to use whenever the study has one.
screens.instead: Keep both rows; make the belief: For most, with it, their last daily log that ate hours in the trailer after the walks would have given them hours back at the end of the day and action items to the crew the same day.

screens.why1: Right after what it does better, asking what my supers have to take on to start using it is the obvious next question before I pick the effort to test.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' and the 9-word limit are plain, and I can answer in my own trade's words without a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a super has to change on the walk and before the log goes out, because I built the product around it.
screens.why4: A free box for up to four efforts with an 'I'm not sure' chip is the right shape, and the escape fits a founder who can't name the effort.
screens.why5: Both rows are my words: supers say who owns each item while filming (the Alex example) and review the notes before they're texted or pushed to Procore, and nothing leaks.
screens.why7: Two efforts, each at most 9 words, base-form verbs in their voice, each a step the super takes themselves; neither repeats Compatibility (filming and talking on the walk) or Purchase friction, and 'Check and fix' reads as one review step rather than two efforts.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what supers will have to do to start, Keel shows the efforts it drafted for me to check, which is exactly where this belongs.
screens.why2: 'Name who owns each item as they film' and 'Check and fix the notes before they go out' are how a super talks about punch items and the log, with no outside-trade words.
screens.why3: Both are things a super does on their own walk and in their own log: calling out who owns the corroded beam, and reading over notes before they hit Procore or the crew's texts.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one while filming and one after, each in a super's words, with no overlap and nothing silly in the list.
screens.why5: Naming the owner matches my assignees and checking the notes fits the sceptics, but the main habit I ask of supers, filming short clips and talking over them on the walk, has dropped off this list and now sits only in Compatibility's 'could'.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form, use the 'their' voice, are under 9 words, and are steps the super takes themselves rather than a sign-off or setup someone else does; neither repeats Purchase friction, and the count is within 1 to 4.
screens.instead: Rows: Film short clips and talk over them on walks · Name who owns each item as they film · Check and fix the notes before they go out

screens.why1: Right after I listed and checked the efforts of starting Fresco, picking the one most likely to stop a super is the obvious next step before the stranger's test.
screens.why2: Naming who owns each item and checking notes before they go out to the crew or Procore is how supers already talk about punch items and logs.
screens.why3: Both are things a super does on their own walk and in their own trailer, so I can judge them from what I know of my customers.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts in trade words, both real catches (assigning on camera, and checking the AI's notes the thread's sceptics worried about), with nothing missing from my list.
screens.why5: Both rows are my mechanism as I described it, with notes carrying assignees and the super sending them out, and the pick is the one I made.
screens.why7: Each row is one base-form effort of at most 9 words in their voice that the super takes themselves, none repeats Compatibility's filming-and-talking or Purchase friction, and the belief can be held or refuted by Yes/Only if against Probably not/No.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious place to decide whether to ask strangers for a real trial, and as a founder hunting commercial GCs for pilots I want this.
screens.why2: Offer a pilot, yes or no, and the hint shows the exact line people will see, so it reads plain on the first pass.
screens.why3: Whether I want emails from supers who would try Fresco is my own call, made from my own goals.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it completely, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: The pilot line asks a superintendent to leave an email for a trial, but I sell per site to the contractor and my commitment step is a paid pilot on one site, so the super's 'try this for real' drifts a little from what I'd actually close.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Respondents who say yes see: "Would you try this on one of your jobs? Leave your email." -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my supers the questions is an obvious last step before the link goes out, right after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: Mostly clear, but the screen says I'm choosing a voice while the interviewer is on video and my pick was the face, so I'd read it twice to know whether I'm picking a face, a voice or both.
screens.why3: It's my own call as founder about how my study reaches superintendents, and I know they'll get it by text and may tap rather than talk from a trailer or a loud site.
screens.why4: Two named interviewers with a preview each and a preselected default is complete and distinct for a pick like this; no escape is needed.
screens.why5: Nothing here rewords my problem, solution or roles, and none of Fresco's product leaks to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask construction superintendents your questions on video? Daphne is picked for you; play Saskia to see and hear her and switch. (Daphne ▶ 5 s · Saskia ▶ 5 s)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, deciding how supers answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'AI interviewer' and 'tap' are clear to a founder and the descriptions say exactly what each means.
screens.why3: I know my supers are on phones in a trailer or truck at the end of the day, so I can judge which format they'll actually finish.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete choices (video AI, text, or let them pick), each described in a line; no escape is needed for a founder's setting.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks, and 'Read and tap' is what I picked and still means what I chose.

screens.why1: Once the interview method is set, choosing who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly to a founder who has been walking job sites and collecting super contacts; 'open link' and 'Contacts page' are clear in context.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I'd send this to: the supers and GCs I've met driving around Napa and the South Bay, by name.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover how I'd reach supers, but the screen doesn't say whether the contractor operations leads for Part 3 go through the same choice or a separate one, which matters for a two-link study.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed here; my pick 'People I know by name' is kept as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link — the superintendents, and separately the contractor ops leads? (People I know by name / People I found with Keel / A group, with one open link)

screens.why_b1: Too few to call is stated at the top and on every card, with 4 counted against 5 needed right beside it, so I know nothing is called yet and why.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, but the tally and cards show the count over 7 and the bar of 5 plainly; I need a second look at the kicker to see that 3 of 7 were not counted, and it never says why.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and the compatibility and adoption lines are mine, but the solution statement repeats itself, with notes and Procore twice, and relative advantage says hours back rather than notes done during the walk, 90% faster.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, such as getting at least one more counted superintendent per belief, or which belief is closest to deciding.
screens.why_b5: It calls nothing with 4 people, keeps 7 answered and 4 counted visible, and says too few on every card.
screens.instead: Not called yet: 4 of 7 superintendents counted on each belief and 5 are needed, so get at least one more superintendent who walked a site this week to answer, and here is why the other 3 were not counted.

screens.why_b1: The status Too few to call sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted and 5 needed, and the So line repeats it.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count 4 people's answers, but the strip's 'your bar, 4 of 5' with the marker at 4 mixes the floor of 5 with the 1-in-3 bar, so I had to look twice to see where my bar sits.
screens.why_b3: The condition is my row word for word, but the belief drops 'on commercial jobs', and the question asks about my last daily log, not the site walk my occasion now names.
screens.why_b4: Asking Ray about his No is a concrete step, but the card never says I need one more counted answer to get a call, and the closing quote about subs and cranes has nothing to do with talking over the noise.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the card says 'a lean, not a call', but '4 of 5' beside my bar reads as if 4 of 5 had said yes, and asking about the daily log rather than the walk softens what the answers mean.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 counted could talk over the noise on their last site walk, and one more answer is needed; ask Ray what stopped him on the walk, and put the bar at no more than 1 in 3 saying only sometimes or no.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats the same tie.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts 3 better (all a lot) and 1 same out of 4, but the strip labels 'your bar · 4 of 5' with the marker at 4, which mixes the 5-person floor with the 1-in-3 bar, and I had to read it twice to see that 1 of 4 is under the bar.
screens.why_b3: Both of my benefits are there, but the belief and the question hang on 'their last daily log', a routine log rather than the day the log cost them, and the bar line names only 'hours back at the end of the day', dropping action items to the crew.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me to get one more counted answer, or that a 3-to-1 lean would clear the bar if it holds, or that Denise's quote says the log isn't her pain at all.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the low n is flagged as 'a lean, not a call', but 'your bar · 4 of 5' under the chart can be misread as four of five people for me when only three were.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know why there is no verdict yet.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count answers among the 5 who answered, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a marker at 4 reads like a 4-of-5-for threshold, which clashes with the 'no more than 1 in 3 against' rule; I had to read it twice to see the 5 is the floor.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would name who owns each item as they film' are my step as I set it, though the 'You said name who owns...' bar line is clumsy.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not say I need one more counted superintendent, or that two of my three yeses hang on naming owners not slowing the walk, which is the thing I would actually go fix.
screens.why_b5: The screen keeps n visible (5 answered, 4 counted), says why Luis is out, splits plain yes from conditional yes, and calls it 'a lean, not a call', so nothing claims more than four supers can carry.
screens.instead: 3 of 4 counted would name owners as they film, but 2 only if it keeps the walk moving; one more counted super decides it, so test whether tagging owners slows the walk.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on "Too few to call" with "4 counted · 5 needed to call it" right beside it, so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: Both belief lines are the ones I checked: talking into the phone over site noise, and hours back plus same-day action items to the crew.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, not even "get one more superintendent to answer" or which of my claims these two No's put at risk.
screens.why_b5: Every count is visible: 4 counted, 1 against, 1 asked why, a single quote each, and the screen calls nothing beyond that.
screens.why_b6: Ray's "the log can wait till morning, the deck can't" and Denise's log done on the tablet before the gate, with schedule and subs eating her day, tell me what I did not write: for some supers the log is neither urgent nor the pain.
screens.instead: Too few to call (4 of 5): one more answer decides it. Both No's say the log isn't the pain, because the schedule and subs are, so check that before the noise question.

screens.why1: It's the first screen and it checks right away whether my job is on Procore or ACC, which is the obvious gate before asking about my daily logs.
screens.why2: Procore and ACC are the platforms I work in every day, and 'jobs you are running' is how a super talks, so I'd answer without a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what platform my own job runs on, because I'm the one uploading the photos and logs into it.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with no overlap, and a gate rightly has no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's Procore-or-ACC segment and gives me nothing about the product or its plan.
screens.why6: The question itself says fine, but 'I'll read 2 options' before a plain yes-or-no sounds stiff when the screener should just end with 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Does the job you're running now run on Procore or ACC? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming my jobs are on Procore, asking whether I lost hours to photo uploads this week is the obvious next thing to ask a super.
screens.why2: Trailer, site photos, uploading: that's exactly how I'd say it, and I get it on one read.
screens.why3: I know whether I sat there pushing photos into Procore this week, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it and I can truly say either; the chips are about the log story that comes after, not this gate.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but 'in the trailer' adds a place; some weeks I upload from the truck or at home at night, and then I'd have to say No even though I lost the same hours.
screens.why6: One short question, then 'Yes or no'; easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: It's the costly act, not the routine, so both Yes and No are true of someone and the belief can go either way; but the added 'in the trailer' bends the clause, so a super who had the problem somewhere else answers No.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you spend hours uploading site photos? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I spent hours in the trailer uploading photos, showing me a tool for the site walk is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Site walk, action items, assignees, Procore and ACC are all my words, but nobody on a job calls anything a 'scribe', and hearing it three times makes it sound like a gimmick.
screens.why3: I walk the site every day, shoot photos, hand out items to the subs and put it all in Procore, so I can picture this exactly.
screens.why4: A card to read, no options.
screens.why5: The last line only repeats the name ('your scribe') instead of saying what it would save me, and it never mentions the daily log, which is what my evenings actually go to.
screens.why6: Short sentences one after another, nothing in brackets or slashes, and 'Procore or ACC' says fine to a super.
screens.instead: Imagine Fresco, an app that turns your site walk videos into the daily log. You talk over short videos as you walk, and it writes up the notes with photos, who's on it and when it's due, texts the crew their items, and sends it to Procore or ACC in one click. The people building it believe it would save you the hours in the trailer uploading and writing up the day.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, it makes sense to ask whether I could actually talk into my phone out on the job, since the whole thing depends on that.
screens.why2: The words are mine, but 'think of your last daily log' made me stop for a second: I write the log in the trailer, and the talking would happen on the walk, so I had to work out which moment they meant.
screens.why3: I walk the site every day with saws, compressors and the crane going, so I know right away whether I could have narrated into my phone.
screens.why4: Easily, most of the time, only sometimes and no cover it without overlap, and 'I can't tell' is a fair way out.
screens.why5: The scribe idea is shown on purpose in the card, and the question itself carries no product talk, just me and my phone on site.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold after hearing them once.
screens.why7: It asks about an ability on the four-rung could-you scale with I can't tell set apart, and it tests the step the pitch rests on, which some supers can manage and some can't over the noise, so the answers can go either way.
screens.instead: Think of your last site walk. Could you have talked into your phone over the noise on site? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the talking-on-site question, asking whether Fresco would have beaten how I did my last log is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: I follow it, but 'keep an accurate record of the day's work on site' is office phrasing; I'd just say 'my daily log', and 'scribe' isn't a word anyone on a job site uses.
screens.why3: I write a daily log every working day and know exactly how the last one went, so I can judge whether turning walk videos into notes would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, and worse cover it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' fits for a super who never shoots video on walks.
screens.why5: No benefit leaks, but the founder's job line is pasted in word for word as the occasion, which reads like their pitch rather than my day.
screens.why6: The stem runs about 35 words with the idea's description said again in the middle, so by the time the four options come I've half lost what log I'm supposed to be thinking of.
screens.why7: The four fixed options with the escape apart are right and the belief can be supported or refuted, but the occasion is the routine job (any daily log) rather than the hurt (the log that ate hours uploading photos), so a super whose last log went fine answers 'no difference' to the wrong question.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent daily log that cost you hours uploading photos in the trailer. Would Fresco, an AI scribe for site walk videos, have done that better, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after asking whether Fresco would do my daily log better, it makes sense to ask what it would cost me on the walk to use it.
screens.why2: Naming who owns each item is how I already talk on a walk ('that's the drywall guy's, that's electrical'), so I get it on one hearing.
screens.why3: I walk the site every day and call out which sub has which issue, so I know whether I'd say it out loud while filming.
screens.why4: Yes, a conditional yes, probably not and no are distinct, and 'only if it keeps the walk moving' is my real catch, because I can't stop at every item to narrate.
screens.why5: Apart from the idea card shown on purpose, nothing of anyone's product talk reaches me, and 'who owns each item' is jobsite language, not a pitch.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options and one escape, easy to hold when heard once.
screens.why7: The effort is a new habit I take myself during the walk, the condition is mine and specific to this step, the options split two for and two against, and 'I can't tell' sits apart as the card requires.
